What is Azure DevOps, and how do its com: Azure DevOps is Microsoft's integrated suite covering the full software delivery lifecycle: Boards for work item/sprint tracking, Repos for Git source control, Pipelines for CI/CD, Artifacts for package management (npm/NuGet/Maven/universal packages), and Test Plans for manual/exploratory test tracking - the integration value is that a Pipeline run can be linked back to the Boards work item it implements and the Repos commit that triggered it, giving end-to-end traceability from a ticket to the exact deployed change, all within one product rather than stitching together separate tools.
Explain an Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline: An Azure Pipeline is structured as Stages (major phases like Build, Deploy-Staging, Deploy-Prod, which can depend on each other and run sequentially or in parallel), each containing Jobs (a unit of work run on a single agent), each containing Steps (individual tasks or scripts) - this three-level nesting is structurally very similar to GitHub Actions' Jobs-containing-Steps model, with Azure's Stages roughly mapping to GitHub Actions' ability to have jobs depend on each other via `needs`, though Azure's explicit Stage concept gives a clearer built-in notion of environment-based promotion than GitHub Actions has natively.
How would you set up a multi-stage Azure: Define a Stage per environment with `dependsOn` chaining them in order, and configure Environments in Azure DevOps (a first-class resource representing a deployment target) with approval checks attached directly to the Environment - so any Stage deploying to the 'production' Environment automatically requires the configured approvers to sign off before it proceeds, without needing custom logic in the pipeline YAML itself, since the gate lives on the Environment resource rather than being hand-coded per pipeline.
What is an Azure DevOps Service Connecti: A Service Connection is Azure DevOps' abstraction for authenticating to an external system (a cloud provider, a Kubernetes cluster, a Docker registry) from within a pipeline, storing the connection's credentials centrally rather than scattered across individual pipeline YAML files. For GCP or AWS, the secure modern approach is workload identity federation (Azure DevOps supports OIDC-based federated credentials) rather than a long-lived service account key or IAM access key - the pipeline exchanges Azure DevOps' own OIDC token for short-lived cloud credentials at runtime, so no static cloud credential is ever stored in Azure DevOps at all.
How do Azure Pipelines templates work, a: A template is a reusable YAML file (stage, job, or step templates) that other pipelines reference via the `template:` keyword, optionally passing parameters - stored in a shared repository and referenced across many teams' pipelines by path and Git ref/tag, similar in purpose to a Jenkins Shared Library or a GitHub Actions reusable workflow. This centralizes common logic (a standard build-and-scan sequence, a standard deploy sequence) so a fix or new security step added to the template propagates to every consuming pipeline through a version bump, rather than needing to be copy-pasted and manually updated across dozens of pipeline files.
How would you troubleshoot an Azure Pipe: Check the agent pool's queue depth and current parallel job usage against your organization's parallel job limit first - Microsoft-hosted agents have a capped concurrency (often just one free parallel job by default, requiring a paid increase or self-hosted agents for real throughput), so a burst of concurrent runs queuing up is often simply hitting that ceiling rather than an actual infrastructure problem. Fix by increasing the parallel job limit (a billing/licensing change) or scaling out a self-hosted agent pool (e.g. auto-scaling VM scale set agents or Kubernetes-based agents) so capacity actually grows with demand instead of being fixed.
What is Azure Artifacts, and how would y: Azure Artifacts is a package registry supporting npm, NuGet, Maven, Python, and universal packages, letting teams publish internal packages/libraries and consume them the same way they'd consume a public package, but privately and access-controlled within the organization. You'd configure feeds (potentially per team or per project) with upstream sources enabled so requests for a public package not found in the internal feed transparently fall through to the public registry (npmjs, PyPI) and get cached - giving both private package hosting and a resilience/caching layer against public registry outages in one feature.
How would you migrate a set of Azure Dev: Basic build/test steps map over fairly mechanically (a script step is a script step in either system), but Azure's explicit Environments-with-approval-checks concept needs to be redesigned using GitHub's Environments feature (which supports required reviewers similarly, but with different configuration syntax), and Azure Pipeline templates need to be re-expressed as GitHub Actions reusable workflows or composite actions - the underlying concepts (stages/jobs/steps, environment gating, reusable templates) exist in both platforms, so migration is more about translating equivalent concepts into GitHub's specific YAML syntax than a fundamental redesign of the deployment logic itself.
What is AWS CodePipeline, and how do Cod: CodePipeline is AWS's orchestration service defining a release process as a sequence of stages, with each stage typically backed by a different AWS service: a Source stage (CodeCommit, or GitHub/other external source) triggers the pipeline on a new commit, a Build stage (CodeBuild) compiles/tests/packages the code, and a Deploy stage (CodeDeploy, or a CloudFormation/ECS deploy action) applies the built artifact to the target environment - CodePipeline itself doesn't build or deploy anything directly, it's purely the orchestration layer coordinating these specialized services and passing artifacts between them.
How does AWS CodeBuild's buildspec.yml w: A buildspec.yml defines phases (install, pre_build, build, post_build) each with a list of shell commands to run, plus an `artifacts` section specifying what output files to package for the next pipeline stage - conceptually equivalent to a GitHub Actions workflow's steps or a Jenkinsfile's stages, just YAML-based and scoped specifically to the build/test/package phase rather than the full pipeline (CodeBuild is one stage within a broader CodePipeline, not the whole pipeline orchestrator itself, which is the key structural difference from a Jenkinsfile that typically defines an entire end-to-end pipeline in one file).
How does AWS CodeDeploy perform a blue-g: For EC2, CodeDeploy provisions a full replacement Auto Scaling group with the new application revision, shifts traffic from the original (blue) group to the new (green) group at the load balancer once health checks pass, and terminates the original group after a configurable bake time - for ECS, it similarly creates a new task set running the new revision, shifts traffic via the load balancer's target groups, and removes the old task set afterward. Both follow the same blue-green principle (full parallel environment, traffic cutover, old environment retained briefly for fast rollback) - CodeDeploy handles the orchestration mechanics so you don't have to script the traffic-shifting and health-check-gating logic yourself.
What is AWS CodeArtifact, and when would: CodeArtifact is AWS's managed package registry (npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, generic) with the same upstream-fallback-to-public-registry pattern as other cloud-native package managers - private packages hosted centrally, public packages transparently proxied and cached. Choose it over a third-party registry (Artifactory, Nexus) when you want tight native IAM-based access control and no separate infrastructure to operate, at the cost of being AWS-specific; a third-party registry makes more sense if you need multi-cloud portability or already operate one for other reasons (e.g. also serving Docker images, which CodeArtifact doesn't support).
How would you design a CI/CD pipeline en: Source stage triggers on a commit (CodeCommit or GitHub), a CodeBuild stage builds the Docker image, runs tests, and pushes it to ECR tagged with the commit SHA, then a Deploy stage applies the new image to EKS - since CodeDeploy's native blue-green support targets EC2/ECS/Lambda rather than raw EKS deployments directly, the EKS deploy stage is typically a CodeBuild action running `kubectl`/`helm` commands (or triggering an external GitOps sync) rather than a native CodeDeploy action, which is an important nuance to know: CodeDeploy doesn't natively understand Kubernetes the way it does ECS.
How would you troubleshoot a CodeBuild j: Check CodeBuild's own compute allocation first - an intermittent, unexplained failure (not a consistent code/test error) is often a resource-starved build environment (an undersized compute type causing an OOM kill mid-build, especially for memory-heavy build steps like large frontend bundling) or a transient network issue reaching an external dependency (a flaky package registry, a rate-limited API call during the build) - CodeBuild's CloudWatch Logs and its own build environment metrics (memory/CPU utilization during the failed run) usually reveal which of these it actually was, rather than the build's own stdout showing a clear application-level error.
How do CodePipeline manual approval acti: Add a Manual Approval action as a stage (or a step within a stage) positioned before the production Deploy stage - the pipeline execution pauses at that action, optionally notifying specified approvers via SNS, and only proceeds once someone with the required IAM permission approves (or the pipeline is stopped if rejected) - the approval action, approver identity, and any comments are recorded in the pipeline's execution history, giving the same kind of auditable gate as an approval stage in any other CI/CD platform.
How does GitHub Actions OIDC-based Workl: GitHub Actions can generate a short-lived OIDC token for a workflow run, cryptographically signed and containing claims about the run (repo, branch, workflow). You configure a trust relationship on the cloud provider's side (an AWS IAM Identity Provider, a GCP Workload Identity Pool, an Azure federated credential) that trusts GitHub's OIDC issuer and validates specific claims (e.g. only tokens from a specific repo and branch) - the cloud provider then exchanges that validated token for short-lived, scoped credentials at runtime, so no static AWS access key, GCP service account key, or Azure client secret ever needs to be stored as a GitHub secret at all.
How would you configure an Azure DevOps: Create a Service Connection of type 'Azure Resource Manager' selecting the 'Workload Identity federation' authentication method rather than 'Service principal (manual)' with a client secret - Azure DevOps generates a federated credential configuration that you register on an Azure AD App Registration, establishing trust between Azure DevOps' own OIDC issuer and that specific App Registration/service principal, scoped to that specific Service Connection. At pipeline run time, Azure DevOps presents its OIDC token, Azure AD validates and exchanges it for a short-lived access token - eliminating the client secret (and its expiration/rotation burden) entirely.
What's the difference between AWS IAM Ro: They're the same underlying mechanism applied to two different OIDC issuers: IRSA trusts the EKS cluster's own OIDC issuer, letting a Kubernetes Pod's service account assume an IAM role by presenting a projected service account token validated against that cluster's issuer. GitHub Actions federation instead trusts GitHub's OIDC issuer, letting a specific workflow run assume an IAM role by presenting GitHub's signed token. Both are instances of the same general pattern (AWS IAM trusting an external OIDC identity provider and exchanging its token for a scoped, short-lived AWS credential) - just with a different, workload-specific issuer on the other side of the trust relationship.
How would you design a CI/CD pipeline's: Use ephemeral, auto-scaling compute for CI/CD executors rather than a fixed pool of always-on agents - Kubernetes-based Jenkins agents (a fresh Pod per build, torn down after), GitHub Actions' own hosted runners (which already scale elastically per-job with no idle cost) or self-hosted runners via an autoscaling controller, or CodeBuild's inherently on-demand compute model (you're billed per build-minute, not for idle capacity). The common thread is treating pipeline compute the same as any other elastic workload - provisioned on demand per job and torn down immediately after, rather than a static pool sized for peak load that sits mostly idle.
